units.text: INT. WOMAN - CONTINUOUS
Oh! . . . yes. I see that. It is very, very helpful. Do you think, Mrs. Allonby, I shall ever meet the Ideal Man? Or are there more than one?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: There are just four in London, Lady Stutfield.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Oh, my dear!
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Going over to her .
What has happened? Do tell me.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: LADY HUNSTANTON [ in a low voice ] I had completely forgotten that the American young lady has been in the room all the time.
I am afraid some of this clever talk may have shocked her a little.
Ah, that will do her so much good!
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Let us hope she didn’t understand much. I think I had better go over and talk to her.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Rises and goes across to HESTER WORSLEY.
Well, dear Miss Worsley.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Sitting down beside her .
How quiet you have been in your nice little corner all this time! I suppose you have been reading a book? There are so many books here in the library.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: No, I have been listening to the conversation.
units.name: HESTER

units.text: You mustn’t believe everything that was said, you know, dear.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: I didn’t believe any of it.
units.name: HESTER

units.text: That is quite right, dear.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Continuing .
I couldn’t believe that any women could really hold such views of life as I have heard to-night from some of your guests.
units.name: HESTER

units.text: An awkward pause .
I hear you have such pleasant society in America. Quite like our own in places, my son wrote to me.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: There are cliques in America as elsewhere, Lady Hunstanton. But true American society consists simply of all the good women and good men we have in our country.
units.name: HESTER

units.text: What a sensible system, and I dare say quite pleasant too. I am afraid in England we have too many artificial social barriers. We don’t see as much as we should of the middle and lower classes.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: In America we have no lower classes.
units.name: HESTER

units.text: Really? What a very strange arrangement!
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: What is that dreadful girl talking about?
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: She is painfully natural, is she not?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: There are a great many things you haven’t got in America, I am told, Miss Worsley. They say you have no ruins, and no curiosities.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: To LADY STUTFIELD.
What nonsense! They have their mothers and their manners.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: The English aristocracy supply us with our curiosities, Lady Caroline. They are sent over to us every summer, regularly, in the steamers, and propose to us the day after they land. As for ruins, we are trying to build up something that will last longer than brick or stone.
units.name: HESTER

units.text: Gets up to take her fan from table .
What is that, dear? Ah, yes, an iron Exhibition, is it not, at that place that has the curious name?
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Standing by table .

We are trying to build up life, Lady Hunstanton, on a better, truer, purer basis than life rests on here. This sounds strange to you all, no doubt. How could it sound other than strange? You rich people in England, you don’t know how you are living. How could you know? You shut out from your society the gentle and the good. You laugh at the simple and the pure. Living, as you all do, on others and by them, you sneer at self-sacrifice, and if you throw bread to the poor, it is merely to keep them quiet for a season. With all your pomp and wealth and art you don’t know how to live—you don’t even know that. You love the beauty that you can see and touch and handle, the beauty that you can destroy, and do destroy, but of the unseen beauty of life, of the unseen beauty of a higher life, you know nothing. You have lost life’s secret. Oh, your English society seems to me shallow, selfish, foolish. It has blinded its eyes, and stopped its ears. It lies like a leper in purple. It sits like a dead thing smeared with gold. It is all wrong, all wrong.
units.name: HESTER

units.text: I don’t think one should know of these things. It is not very, very nice, is it?
units.name: LADY STUTFIELD

units.text: My dear Miss Worsley, I thought you liked English society so much. You were such a success in it. And you were so much admired by the best people. I quite forget what Lord Henry Weston said of you—but it was most complimentary, and you know what an authority he is on beauty.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Lord Henry Weston! I remember him, Lady Hunstanton. A man with a hideous smile and a hideous past. He is asked everywhere. No dinner-party is complete without him. What of those whose ruin is due to him? They are outcasts. They are nameless. If you met them in the street you would turn your head away. I don’t complain of their punishment. Let all women who have sinned be punished.
units.name: HESTER

units.text: MRS. ARBUTHNOT enters from terrace behind in a cloak with a lace veil over her head .
She hears the last words and starts .
My dear young lady!
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: It is right that they should be punished, but don’t let them be the only ones to suffer. If a man and woman have sinned, let them both go forth into the desert to love or loathe each other there. Let them both be branded. Set a mark, if you wish, on each, but don’t punish the one and let the other go free. Don’t have one law for men and another for women. You are unjust to women in England. And till you count what is a shame in a woman to be an infamy in a man, you will always be unjust, and Right, that pillar of fire, and Wrong, that pillar of cloud, will be made dim to your eyes, or be not seen at all, or if seen, not regarded.
units.name: HESTER

units.text: Might I, dear Miss Worsley, as you are standing up, ask you for my cotton that is just behind you? Thank you.
units.name: LADY CAROLINE

units.text: My dear Mrs. Arbuthnot! I am so pleased you have come up. But I didn’t hear you announced.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Oh, I came straight in from the terrace, Lady Hunstanton, just as I was. You didn’t tell me you had a party.
units.name: MRS. ALLONBY

units.text: Not a party. Only a few guests who are staying in the house, and whom you must know. Allow me.
units.name: LADY HUNSTANTON

units.text: Tries to help her .
Rings bell .
